summary: Describes a way for an L2TP Access Controller to tell the L2TP Network Server that a client modem has put its call on hold, a modem feature that lets the phone line be used for other calls and the link later resume without redialing. The base protocol had no way to signal this. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: On a dial-up connection, you could pause the link to take a phone call and then resume. This memo lets the far end know that the pause is happening, so it does not hang up.

questions: what is l2tp modem on hold

what is v92 modem on hold
what does an lns do when a modem is on hold
subtitle: How an L2TP access concentrator tells the network server that a dial-up modem has put its call on hold.

tldr.problem: A V.92 modem can put its call on hold and resume later without redialing, but the L2TP base protocol gives the LAC no way to tell the LNS this has happened.
tldr.mechanism: The LNS advertises a Modem On-Hold Capable AVP when the tunnel is set up, and the LAC then sends a Modem-Status (MDMST) control message carrying a Modem On-Hold Status AVP with a hold bit and a timeout.
tldr.outcome: The LNS learns when the modem goes on hold and returns online, but the RFC leaves what to do with that information to the implementation.

today: RFC 3573 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on L2TP as defined in RFC 2661.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
The Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol (RFC 2661) tunnels PPP sessions. Those sessions are often set up with modems over the public switched telephone network. ITU-T Recommendation V.92 lets a client modem put the call on hold and later re-establish the link without redialing, and the phone line can be used for another call in the meantime.

The L2TP base protocol cannot signal these events from the LAC (L2TP Access Controller), where the modem is connected, to the LNS (L2TP Network Server), where the PPP session is handled. This document adds AVPs and a control message to carry that information. It does not define what, if anything, the LNS should do with it.
sections.plainLanguage: The modem end knows when you pause the call, but the far end of the tunnel does not. This memo adds a way to pass the word along.

sections.title: Topology and Usage Scenario
sections.content:
In the dial-in topology a remote system with a client modem (M) reaches a server modem (SM) at the LAC through the telephone network. The LAC connects across a packet network to the LNS. If the client modem implements V.92, it can ask the server modem whether the call may be placed on hold for some period. If the server modem agrees, the client signals the telephone network, usually with a flash hook, and the user can use the same line for another call.

The memo's example is a user downloading a large file who receives a call, tells the modem to go on hold, talks, and then returns to the original call with another flash hook so the download continues.

The LNS MUST NOT stop processing otherwise valid data packets arriving from the LAC, whatever the current on-hold indications say.
sections.plainLanguage: You are downloading something and a friend calls. Your modem tells the other modem to wait, you chat, and afterwards the download picks up where it left off.

sections.title: Capability Negotiation
sections.content: A LAC MUST NOT send a Modem-Status message to an LNS that has not said it can process it. The LNS says so by including a Modem On-Hold Capable AVP (Attribute Type 53) in the SCCRQ or SCCRP control message sent to the LAC when the tunnel comes up. The AVP has no Attribute Value field, a Length of 6 and its M-bit MUST be 0. It MAY be hidden.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending news about pauses, the LAC checks that the other side said it wants to hear them.

sections.title: The Modem-Status Message
sections.content:
The Modem-Status (MDMST) control message uses Vendor ID 0 and Attribute Type 17, and the Message Type AVP and Modem On-Hold Status AVP MUST be present. It MUST be sent with the M-bit in the Message Type AVP set to 0, so peers that do not know it ignore it.

When the client modem asks to go on hold, the LAC SHOULD send MDMST with the H (Hold) field set to 1 and the negotiated maximum on-hold time. When the modem comes back, the LAC SHOULD send MDMST with H set to 0, and MUST do so if it earlier sent H set to 1.

MDMST can only be sent after session establishment succeeds (after the LAC sent ICCN or OCCN) and before the session ends (before the LAC sent or received CDN). Because of races, an LNS MUST ignore MDMST received after it sent a CDN, and MUST ignore redundant status reports.
sections.plainLanguage: The LAC sends a short note saying paused when the modem pauses and back when it returns. Late or repeated notes are ignored.

sections.title: The Modem On-Hold Status AVP
sections.content: The Modem On-Hold Status AVP (Attribute Type 54) is a 16-bit value. The H (Hold) bit is 1 when the client modem is on hold and 0 when it is back online. The 4-bit Timeout field gives the negotiated maximum time on hold, using values defined in V.92. It is valid only when H is 1 and MUST be ignored when H is 0. Bits 1 through 11 are reserved: they MUST be 0 when sending and ignored on reception. The AVP MAY be hidden, its M-bit MUST be 0, and its Length is 8.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a tiny two-part note: one switch for on-hold or not, and a number for how long the hold may last.

sections.title: What an LNS Might Do
sections.content:
The specific actions are implementation dependent. Choices can affect higher layer protocols, since TCP connections may time out or disconnect during the hold. The memo lists possible actions: temporarily stop polling protocols such as LCP Echo Requests, Link Quality Monitoring and Multilink PPP; drop data packets for the on-hold client; start a new accounting session; stop or hold accounting; or account separately for hold time.

It also lists things an LNS should probably not do: buffer packets for the on-hold client, answer TCP keepalives in place of the client, or stop processing valid data packets from the client. The last one is because the online notification and the first client packet travel on independent channels, and dropping valid packets slows recovery through forced retries.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo suggests a few things the far end could do while you are paused, and a few it should avoid, like holding on to messages for you.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: The document requires one new L2TP Message Type number, 17 for Modem Status, and two new AVP Attributes, 53 for Modem On-Hold Capable and 54 for Modem On-Hold Status. The reserved bits 1 through 11 of the status AVP are assigned by IANA through IETF Consensus. Appendix A, which is not normative, records vendor-specific values with Vendor ID 529 used by early implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The new message and settings get official numbers so everyone uses the same ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Integrity and confidentiality rely on the underlying L2TP security mechanisms. The extension only indicates when a client modem has gone on hold and cannot receive data, and it is believed not to give an attacker useful information. If desired, the new AVPs MAY be hidden as described in section 4.3 of RFC 2661.
sections.plainLanguage: The news that a modem is paused is not very secret, and the existing tunnel protections still apply.

messages.label: SCCRQ or SCCRP + Modem On-Hold Capable

fields.name: H
fields.desc: 1 if the client modem is on hold, 0 if back online.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Bits 1 through 11. Sent as 0, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Timeout
fields.desc: Negotiated maximum hold time; valid only if H is 1.
